title: Iran mediators push new ceasefire as Trump eyes all-out war
description: President Trump is nearing a decisive fork in the Iran war, with U.S. and Israeli officials envisioning only two viable endgames: Option 1: Pursue a new 10-day ceasefire aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz . Option 2: Launch a massive joint military campaign with Israel to force Tehran's capitulation. Why it matters: Trump hasn't made a decision yet. But officials believe the next few days will determine which path prevails — with little room left for the grinding, open-ended conflict now paralyzing the Gulf. Driving the news: Qatar, Egypt, Pakistan and other regional mediators have presented the U.S. and Iran with a proposal for a 10-day ceasefire, two regional sources with direct knowledge of the effort told Axios. The Trump administration is exploring the proposal and has urged Israel to avoid steps that could close the diplomatic window, U.S. officials said. But Washington is simultaneously preparing for the talks to fail. The U.S. military has sent dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft to the region in recent days, assembling the forces needed for a major escalation. Israeli sources said the IDF is on high alert and preparing for a possible expansion of the war into a full-scale, coordinated campaign within days. The big picture: Ten straight nights of U.S. bombing have failed to break Iran's grip on the Strait of Hormuz, dragging Trump deeper into a war he has repeatedly declared won. At least three U.S. service members have been killed in the renewed fighting. Trump said Monday he had ordered the Pentagon to make Iran pay "many times over" for every American death. Oil briefly broke $90 a barrel this weekend as Iran widened its strikes on commercial ships and Gulf infrastructure. Gas prices are rising again, compounding the domestic backlash to an already unpopular war. Zoom in: Regional mediators are once again racing to interrupt a cycle of retaliation that grows deadlier, costlier and harder to contain with each new strike. The new ceasefire proposal would halt the fighting, reopen both shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz, and give Washington and Tehran room to salvage their collapsing memorandum of understanding (MOU). "We told the U.S. and Iran that we propose a cooling-off period," one of the regional sources said. State of play: Neither Trump nor Iran has accepted the proposal, and both sides appear determined to improve their leverage through further strikes before committing to a ceasefire. In the meantime, the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi ports, opening another front against the Gulf's energy infrastructure and shipping lanes. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has warned that Israel will answer any Iranian attack with massive strikes, raising the risk of a wider war stretching from the Gulf to the Red Sea and Israel. Behind the scenes: Regional sources said mediators are trying to build on a proposal discussed by Oman, Iran and Qatar in Muscat, Oman, on July 11, when the U.S. demanded Tehran publicly commit to keeping the Strait of Hormuz open. Those talks ended without an agreement, and Iran attacked commercial ships in the strait shortly afterward — triggering the U.S. bombing campaign that has continued every night since. The proposal would fully reopen both Hormuz shipping lanes: the southern route through Omani waters, free of Iranian attacks, and the northern route through Iranian waters, free of the U.S. blockade. During the 10-day ceasefire, the U.S. and Iran would negotiate a longer-term arrangement governing passage through the strait. One option would allow Iran to collect "reasonable service fees" for maritime security, environmental protection and other services, according to one regional source. The source pointed to the Strait of Malacca — where Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore charge vessels for specific services rather than a blanket transit fee — as a possible model. Another idea would direct the fees into a joint fund administered with the involvement of the International Maritime Organization. Officials involved in the mediation include Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Qatari envoy Ali Al-Thawadi, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi. The intrigue: One regional source said the ceasefire effort was gaining momentum Saturday, before an Iranian missile strike in Jordan killed at least two U.S. service members and prompted Washington to pull back. A senior U.S. official confirmed that talks are continuing but said Trump has yet to finish retaliating. "The president is focused on making Iran pay for its violations of the MOU and its continued acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz," the official told Axios. "In addition, the president will make Iran pay for the recent deaths of U.S. soldiers. These devastating blows will continue until the president deems otherwise." What they're saying: Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei confirmed Monday that mediators were working to prevent further escalation. "The proposals conveyed through the mediators have been received by us, but at this stage I prefer not to discuss their details," Baghaei said at an Iranian press briefing. He added that Iran's armed forces would continue to "respond with strength and crush the source of U.S. aggression." What to watch: It's unclear whether Trump has been fully briefed on the ceasefire framework — or whether he would accept another temporary ceasefire without a clear path toward a lasting settlement. The president has voiced deep frustration with Tehran since the ceasefire collapsed, calling Iran's leaders "sick people" and dismissing further negotiations as a "waste of time." One regional source said the White House may continue bombing Iran for several more days to avenge the killing of the U.S. service members in Jordan before seriously considering the proposal. The bottom line: "We are trying to work out a sustainable solution," one regional source said. "The Iranians can't dictate the terms, but they also can't be ignored."

title: U.S. to slap 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
description: The Trump administration said Monday that it will impose an additional 50% tariff on certain Canadian goods — including hockey sticks, wine and cement — accusing Canada of discriminating against U.S. exports. Why it matters: The move ratchets up tensions in an increasingly bitter trade dispute between two of the world's closest economic partners. Zoom out: The tariffs , which take effect next month, will be imposed under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — a never-before-used authority. The duties cover roughly $20 billion in annual Canadian imports. A senior administration official said the tariffs were not the wildfire tariffs that President Trump had earlier threatened, though the official added that options on that front remain under consideration. Zoom in: The administration says that Canada is one of only two countries — alongside China — to retaliate against Trump's earlier tariffs, pointing to provinces that pulled U.S. liquor from store shelves. Officials also cited auto policies they say favor Canadian production and dairy rules they argue give European cheese an advantage over American imports. The backdrop: Trump threatened to impose additional Canadian tariffs last week in a Truth Social post , saying that costs related to the wildfire smoke must be added to the tariffs. Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney were seen together on Sunday at the World Cup final match in East Rutherford, N.J. Trump told reporters the two men talked about potential action in response to the wildfires while noting their "good relationship." The big picture: This marks another escalation in U.S.-Canada tensions after the Trump administration declined to extend the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement , leaving the continent's trade pact in limbo. Unlike previous Trump tariffs on Canada, the new duties apply to goods that qualify for duty-free treatment under the USMCA. Economists have found that the trade deal has been critical in limiting the tariff impact on consumer prices. The exemptions spare some of Canada's most strategically important exports, including potash, critical minerals and most energy products, limiting the potential fallout for U.S. industry. The other side: In a statement posted on X , Carney called the tariffs "in direct violation" of the USMCA and pledged to intensify negotiations in the coming weeks. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce called the tariffs a "regrettable escalation" and urged both countries to use the month before they take effect to advance negotiations. The intrigue: This year's Supreme Court decision limiting Trump's emergency tariff powers forced the administration to search for other legal avenues to impose its trade agenda. That includes the administration's temporary 10% global tariffs under Section 122 of the Trade Act — an authority that expires later this week. Editor's note: This story was updated with additional details.

title: Senate watches the House on reconciliation 3.0
description: Senate Republicans are warming to the idea of using a third reconciliation package to replenish the Pentagon's depleted weapons stocks. Why it matters: They still view reconciliation 3.0 as Plan B. For now, though, they're willing to let House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) attempt the legislative equivalent of a triple axel: passing a rule, a short-term government funding bill and a budget resolution to unlock reconciliation. "The tale of the tape is going to be what the House can do," Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) said. "Can the House pass it? I don't think that's a done deal. It's not offset, so I think there's going to be some troubled water there." But Republican senators aren't slamming the door on Johnson's plan, looking to keep Senate options open. "It's pretty clear that [Senate Minority Leader Chuck] Schumer would like to play shutdown politics," Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said. "So I don't have any problem with using reconciliation for that." "But beyond that, it gets pretty narrow, what I'd be willing to support." Driving the news: President Trump is ramping up pressure on House Republicans to support the budget resolution ahead of a pivotal week on Capitol Hill. "I am asking all House Republicans to VOTE YES this week on the Budget Resolution, which is an important first step towards getting a Budget Bill," Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social . Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought will try to close the deal at the Republican conference Tuesday. The move is a clear signal the administration wants a fallback plan if the normal appropriations process isn't done by Oct. 1 — which looks increasingly likely. Meanwhile, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will testify before the Senate Appropriations Committee on Tuesday to defend the administration's supplemental funding request, including tens of billions of dollars to replenish munitions used in Iran. Between the lines: Senate Majority Leader John Thune is cautioning that reconciliation 3.0 still faces a steep climb, even if it clears the House. "Easier said than done," Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters. And not every Senate Republican is on board. "I am not a big fan of reconciliation whether it's 1.0, 2.0 or 3.0," Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said . Zoom in: The White House has sent a list of spending anomalies to appropriators — a necessary step for Congress and OMB to advance a short-term continuing resolution. The move is a clear signal that the administration expects Congress to rely on a stopgap spending bill to avert a shutdown. That remains senators' preferred path. "I'd love a clean CR to get us through the election," Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) said. Zoom out: Vice President Vance's private appeal to House Republicans last week did little to change the political math. Johnson faces a difficult challenge. The skepticism extends beyond the House. Some Senate Republicans want a larger package with more defense funding, while others insist that at least some of the roughly $95 billion in new spending be offset. The House proposal includes about $60 billion to replenish munitions and weapons stocks depleted by U.S. operations against Iran. The bottom line: The Senate is waiting on the House while pursuing a two-track strategy: keep appropriations moving while keeping reconciliation in reserve if negotiations break down. "We either need to keep appropriations moving," Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) told Axios, "or it's reconciliation 3.0."

One regional source said the White House may continue bombing Iran for several more days to avenge the killing of the U.S. service members in Jordan before seriously considering the proposal. The bottom line: "We are trying to work out a sustainable solution," one regional source said. "The Iranians can't dictate the terms, but they also can't be ignored."

title: U.S. to slap 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
description: The Trump administration said Monday that it will impose an additional 50% tariff on certain Canadian goods — including hockey sticks, wine and cement — accusing Canada of discriminating against U.S. exports. Why it matters: The move ratchets up tensions in an increasingly bitter trade dispute between two of the world's closest economic partners. Zoom out: The tariffs , which take effect next month, will be imposed under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — a never-before-used authority. The duties cover roughly $20 billion in annual Canadian imports. A senior administration official said the tariffs were not the wildfire tariffs that President Trump had earlier threatened, though the official added that options on that front remain under consideration. Zoom in: The administration says that Canada is one of only two countries — alongside China — to retaliate against Trump's earlier tariffs, pointing to provinces that pulled U.S. liquor from store shelves. Officials also cited auto policies they say favor Canadian production and dairy rules they argue give European cheese an advantage over American imports. The backdrop: Trump threatened to impose additional Canadian tariffs last week in a Truth Social post , saying that costs related to the wildfire smoke must be added to the tariffs. Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney were seen together on Sunday at the World Cup final match in East Rutherford, N.J. Trump told reporters the two men talked about potential action in response to the wildfires while noting their "good relationship." The big picture: This marks another escalation in U.S.-Canada tensions after the Trump administration declined to extend the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement , leaving the continent's trade pact in limbo. Unlike previous Trump tariffs on Canada, the new duties apply to goods that qualify for duty-free treatment under the USMCA. Economists have found that the trade deal has been critical in limiting the tariff impact on consumer prices. The exemptions spare some of Canada's most strategically important exports, including potash, critical minerals and most energy products, limiting the potential fallout for U.S. industry. The other side: In a statement posted on X , Carney called the tariffs "in direct violation" of the USMCA and pledged to intensify negotiations in the coming weeks. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce called the tariffs a "regrettable escalation" and urged both countries to use the month before they take effect to advance negotiations. The intrigue: This year's Supreme Court decision limiting Trump's emergency tariff powers forced the administration to search for other legal avenues to impose its trade agenda. That includes the administration's temporary 10% global tariffs under Section 122 of the Trade Act — an authority that expires later this week. Editor's note: This story was updated with additional details.

title: Senate watches the House on reconciliation 3.0
description: Senate Republicans are warming to the idea of using a third reconciliation package to replenish the Pentagon's depleted weapons stocks. Why it matters: They still view reconciliation 3.0 as Plan B. For now, though, they're willing to let House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) attempt the legislative equivalent of a triple axel: passing a rule, a short-term government funding bill and a budget resolution to unlock reconciliation. "The tale of the tape is going to be what the House can do," Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) said. "Can the House pass it? I don't think that's a done deal. It's not offset, so I think there's going to be some troubled water there." But Republican senators aren't slamming the door on Johnson's plan, looking to keep Senate options open. "It's pretty clear that [Senate Minority Leader Chuck] Schumer would like to play shutdown politics," Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said. "So I don't have any problem with using reconciliation for that." "But beyond that, it gets pretty narrow, what I'd be willing to support." Driving the news: President Trump is ramping up pressure on House Republicans to support the budget resolution ahead of a pivotal week on Capitol Hill. "I am asking all House Republicans to VOTE YES this week on the Budget Resolution, which is an important first step towards getting a Budget Bill," Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social . Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought will try to close the deal at the Republican conference Tuesday. The move is a clear signal the administration wants a fallback plan if the normal appropriations process isn't done by Oct. 1 — which looks increasingly likely. Meanwhile, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will testify before the Senate Appropriations Committee on Tuesday to defend the administration's supplemental funding request, including tens of billions of dollars to replenish munitions used in Iran. Between the lines: Senate Majority Leader John Thune is cautioning that reconciliation 3.0 still faces a steep climb, even if it clears the House. "Easier said than done," Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters. And not every Senate Republican is on board. "I am not a big fan of reconciliation whether it's 1.0, 2.0 or 3.0," Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said . Zoom in: The White House has sent a list of spending anomalies to appropriators — a necessary step for Congress and OMB to advance a short-term continuing resolution. The move is a clear signal that the administration expects Congress to rely on a stopgap spending bill to avert a shutdown. That remains senators' preferred path. "I'd love a clean CR to get us through the election," Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) said. Zoom out: Vice President Vance's private appeal to House Republicans last week did little to change the political math. Johnson faces a difficult challenge. The skepticism extends beyond the House. Some Senate Republicans want a larger package with more defense funding, while others insist that at least some of the roughly $95 billion in new spending be offset. The House proposal includes about $60 billion to replenish munitions and weapons stocks depleted by U.S. operations against Iran. The bottom line: The Senate is waiting on the House while pursuing a two-track strategy: keep appropriations moving while keeping reconciliation in reserve if negotiations break down. "We either need to keep appropriations moving," Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) told Axios, "or it's reconciliation 3.0."
